title: Pickup bands and booking practices
summary: Leaders booked many jobs and sent substitutes; musicians read stocks.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: How big a band was that playing for the district? Probably eight men.
That was quite usual. But I don't remember. There were a lot of halls there that had eight-piece minimums in New York. Who's the leader? Lou Lockman. Lou Lockett. Lou Lockett.

Bill can check that for you. He knows for sure. He knows the name. He's the leader. But with an eight-piece band you could sort of imitate swing a little I guess. Oh, I used to play a lot of jazz. You could choruses all the time, sure. But I mean you could get some, that was a flexible band.
Yeah, but usually you see they played stocks because these bands weren't in any way organized.

As a matter of fact, it was quite customary in New York for a guy to book all the jobs he could. He never turned a job down. He might, if he were really hot or had lucky, he might book say three jobs on a Saturday night. And the reason he booked those jobs was so that he could give two of them to friends of

And so it was nothing for a leader to go in the union hall and hire a band, you know, engage the different musicians. And then when he got on the job he was apt to find that half of them or even more were guys he hadn't seen before. You see, you'd come in and sort of say, Benny sent me here, Joe sent me. And this was alright so long as you cut the job. You didn't jeopardize the connection of the guy that had booked it. This was common practice.
So long as you could read stocks. Read stocks was about all that.

Oh yeah, read the stocks and occasionally the guy might have a few little sheets he'd scratched out and read those and play some jazz if that's what you were supposed to do. We're coming to the end of the tape.
